name: The doctor's garden in Wabansia
aka: the garden 'attached to' the convenient dwelling house in Wabansia (Chicago Democrat, 16 July 1834)

documented_range.note: The garden is attested on the same day and by the same line as the house and the barn (data/structures/wabansia_doctors_house.json), and is carried to the scene date by the same inference. Chicago Democrat, 16 July 1834, p. 3 col. 2 (claim chicago_democrat_1834_07_16#c017): '[A] CONVENIENT Dwelling House, in W[a]bansia, now occupied by Doctor Kimberl[y]. It has four rooms, with a kitchen, barn, an[d] garden attached to it.'

existence.note: THE GARDEN IS ATTESTED; ITS FENCE, ITS SIZE AND ITS PLACE ARE NOT. Chicago Democrat, 16 July 1834, p. 3 col. 2 (claim chicago_democrat_1834_07_16#c017): '[A] CONVENIENT Dwelling House, in W[a]bansia, now occupied by Doctor Kimberl[y]. It has four rooms, with a kitchen, barn, an[d] garden attached to it.' A kitchen garden in a town where hogs ran at large is a fenced one, so the pale is drawn, and it is graded reconstructed below the existence.

runs.note: RECONSTRUCTED, ONE CLOSED RING. A 13 x 17 m plot (about a twentieth of an acre - a household's vegetables, not a market garden) on the river side of the house, between the house's east wall line and the barn, inside the same eastern lot of blk_wabansia_c_t7 the house and barn were placed on. The edges are whole-metre lines chosen to clear the house by 4 m and the barn by 8 m; none is read off any source. Covered by docs/LIBERTIES.md L316.

openings.note: INVENTED. A garden nobody can enter is not a garden, so one gate is drawn, a person's width (3 ft), on the side facing the house's own east wall - the shortest walk from the kitchen ell, which stands at the house's east end.

fence_type.note: BORROWED UNCHANGED from data/enclosures/town_dooryard_pickets.json, whose argument follows. INVENTED, and it is the one value on this record with a picture behind it. The Kinzie-view plate — panel 12 of `kurz_allison_1893`, identified in the existence note — shows PICKETS: close-set vertical pales, not the open horizontal rails this layer draws at the wagon yard and the pound, and that difference is the whole point of the distinction: a rail fence turns a team and a picket fence keeps poultry out of the vegetables. The plate is tier 5 and it is of a house on the north bank that this scene excludes, so it bounds a treatment and attests nothing about these lots.

height_m.note: BORROWED UNCHANGED from data/enclosures/town_dooryard_pickets.json, whose argument follows. INVENTED. 1.22 m is 4 ft, recorded converted. Nothing attests a height. The bound is the use, read against the two fences already in this dataset: a garden pale turns poultry and a rooting hog off a bed of vegetables, which needs less than the Western Hotel's 4 ft 6 in yard fence (that one turns a hitched team) and far less than the pound's 6 ft (that one holds a beast that means to leave). Four feet is the least that does the garden's job. A Chicago or Cook County lawful-fence ordinance of the 1830s would replace this number outright, and this project holds none.

rail_courses.note: BORROWED UNCHANGED from data/enclosures/town_dooryard_pickets.json, whose argument follows. INVENTED. Two stringers is what a pale fence of this height is built on — the pales carry the closure and the rails only hold them in line, which is the opposite of the rail fences on this layer, where the courses ARE the fence. Nothing attests a count.

post_spacing_m.note: BORROWED UNCHANGED from data/enclosures/town_dooryard_pickets.json, whose argument follows. INVENTED. 2.44 m is 8 ft, the same bay as the pound, because it is the same reason — the span a sawn rail of the period is cut to carry. Nothing attests a bay.

post_size_m.note: BORROWED UNCHANGED from data/enclosures/town_dooryard_pickets.json, whose argument follows. INVENTED. A 0.10 m post is a 4-inch stick, the lightest on this layer and lighter than the yard fence's 0.14 m: a garden fence is not leaned on by anything heavier than a gardener. Nothing attests it.

picket_width_m.note: BORROWED UNCHANGED from data/enclosures/town_dooryard_pickets.json, whose argument follows. INVENTED. 0.089 m is 3.5 in — a riven or sawn pale off the same pile of stuff the town's frame houses are boarded from. Nothing attests a pale, its width, or that these fences were made of sawn timber at all.

picket_gap_m.note: BORROWED UNCHANGED from data/enclosures/town_dooryard_pickets.json, whose argument follows. INVENTED. A pale-wide gap is the rhythm the Kinzie-view plate reads as at the scale it is drawn, and it is the number that decides whether this fence looks like a wall or like a fence. Nothing attests it. It is recorded here rather than left to the renderer for the same reason the post rhythm is: the number a visitor is looking at should be one this file states.

ground.note: THE GARDEN IS ATTESTED AND THE BEDS ARE NOT. Drawn with the same dooryard_garden treatment as the town's fifteen dooryard plots (data/enclosures/town_dooryard_pickets.json), because 'garden' in an 1834 house advertisement is the kitchen garden that treatment draws; what grew in it is not stated and nothing is planted by name.

citations.citation: Chicago Democrat, 16 July 1834, p. 3 col. 2 (claim chicago_democrat_1834_07_16#c017): '[A] CONVENIENT Dwelling House, in W[a]bansia, now occupied by Doctor Kimberl[y]. It has four rooms, with a kitchen, barn, an[d] garden attached to it.'

research_note: THE ONE GARDEN IN THE TOWN A PRINTED SOURCE NAMES WITH ITS HOUSE. Everything about its fence and its plot is borrowed from the dooryard-picket rule rather than reasoned again, because nothing distinguishes this garden from those except that this one is attested.
